presentingComplaint: Fever with a rapidly spreading, sharply demarcated red rash over the right shin for 24 hours
history: 61-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia on bendamustine-rituximab (last cycle 11 days ago), presents with a 1-day history of high fever with shaking chills followed by the appearance of a bright, fiery-red, painful patch over the right lower leg that has visibly enlarged over hours. He reports the area feels hot, tense and glossy, with a clearly raised edge he can feel with his finger. There is longstanding scaling and fissuring between the right toes (tinea pedis) that he identifies as the likely portal of entry. No recent trauma, no animal bites, no foreign travel. He is aware his blood counts run low after chemotherapy. No breathlessness, chest pain, abdominal or urinary symptoms. Prior antibiotic exposure: none in the last 90 days. No prior MRSA/ESBL/CRE isolates. He lives at home, independent.
examination: Unwell, flushed and mildly rigoring. Right shin shows a well-circumscribed, raised, indurated, brightly erythematous plaque roughly 12 x 8 cm with a sharply demarcated, palpable advancing border clearly distinct from surrounding normal skin; surface is warm, tense and shiny with early peau d'orange. Marked tenderness on palpation but NO pain out of proportion, no crepitus, no bullae, no skin necrosis and no dusky discolouration. Tender right inguinal lymphadenopathy and a faint ascending lymphangitic streak. Interdigital tinea with fissuring in the right web spaces. Peripheral pulses present, no calf swelling on the contralateral side. Cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination unremarkable.
imaging: Soft-tissue ultrasound of the right leg: dermal and subcutaneous oedema with a 'cobblestone' appearance, NO subcutaneous gas, no drainable collection and no fascial-plane fluid tracking to suggest necrotising infection. No deep venous thrombosis on compression Doppler.
microbiology: Two sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn before antibiotics. Interdigital swab sent. At 36 hours one blood culture set flags Gram-positive cocci in chains; identified as Streptococcus pyogenes (Lancefield group A), penicillin-susceptible. Surface swab grew group A Streptococcus with no Staphylococcus aureus.
differentialDiagnoses: Erysipelas (superficial group A streptococcal dermal infection) - sharply demarcated raised border, fiery erythema, portal of entry via tinea pedis
Cellulitis - deeper, less well-demarcated border with indistinct edge
Necrotizing fasciitis - excluded: no pain out of proportion, no crepitus/bullae, no gas or fascial fluid on imaging
Deep vein thrombosis - excluded on negative compression Doppler
finalDiagnosis: Erysipelas of the right lower limb (group A Streptococcus, penicillin-susceptible) in a chemotherapy-associated neutropenic host, portal of entry interdigital tinea pedis
citations: IDSA - Practical Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections - 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Cellulitis, Erysipelas and Soft-Tissue Infections
stewardship: Erysipelas is caused almost exclusively by beta-haemolytic streptococci (predominantly group A Streptococcus), for which penicillin is the guideline-concordant agent (IDSA SSTI 2014; Harrison 22e). In an ordinary host, targeted penicillin/amoxicillin is first line. Here the patient is febrile and neutropenic (ANC 0.7) following chemotherapy, so initial empiric therapy is appropriately broadened to cover Gram-negatives and Pseudomonas per neutropenic-sepsis principles while streptococcal disease is confirmed - start IV cefepime (anti-pseudomonal, retains streptococcal activity). The classic sharply demarcated erysipelas morphology plus rapidly evolving blood cultures showing group A Streptococcus permit prompt de-escalation: once ANC recovers and cultures return penicillin-susceptible S. pyogenes with clinical improvement, narrow to IV benzylpenicillin, then step down to oral amoxicillin/penicillin V to complete a 5-7 day course. Anti-MRSA and anti-anaerobic cover are not indicated for uncomplicated erysipelas and should not be continued. Treat the tinea pedis portal of entry to prevent recurrence. Escalation to surgical review is warranted only if features of necrotising infection emerge.
contraindications: Penicillin/beta-lactam allergy - verify before benzylpenicillin/cefepime; use clindamycin or a glycopeptide if genuine severe allergy
Avoid unnecessary aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity if renal function borderline
Do not add empiric anti-MRSA (vancomycin/linezolid) or anaerobic cover for uncomplicated erysipelas
edgeCases: Neutropenia can blunt the erythema and systemic response, so a sharply demarcated lesion in a febrile neutropenic patient still mandates urgent broad empiric cover
Failure to improve within 48-72h or emergence of pain out of proportion, bullae or crepitus should trigger reassessment for necrotising fasciitis
Recurrent erysipelas is common if the tinea pedis portal of entry is not treated
expectedMaiK: Recognise the sharply demarcated, raised, fiery-red plaque with a palpable advancing border and lymphangitis as erysipelas (group A streptococcal); understand that penicillin is the definitive concordant therapy, but that a febrile neutropenic host warrants broad empiric anti-pseudomonal cover first, with prompt de-escalation to penicillin once streptococcal disease is confirmed.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there a portal of entry (tinea pedis, fissure, ulcer, recent trauma)?
What is the degree and expected duration of neutropenia and the chemotherapy timeline?
Any features suggesting necrotising infection (pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, rapid systemic deterioration)?
Prior episodes of erysipelas/cellulitis or prior resistant organisms?
expectedInvestigations: Two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics
Full blood count with differential (ANC) and CRP/procalcitonin
Soft-tissue ultrasound to exclude collection/necrotising features and compression Doppler to exclude DVT
Swab of any interdigital fissure/portal of entry

antibiotics: Cefepime IV (empiric broad cover for the febrile neutropenic host)
Benzylpenicillin IV then oral amoxicillin/penicillin V (de-escalation once penicillin-susceptible group A Streptococcus confirmed)

regressionAssertions: Sharply demarcated raised border must be recognised as distinguishing erysipelas from cellulitis
Necrotising fasciitis must be actively excluded and not treated as the primary diagnosis
Definitive therapy must narrow to penicillin for confirmed group A Streptococcus
Empiric anti-pseudomonal cover is justified by febrile neutropenia and must be de-escalated, not continued indefinitely
